interactions.label: In bone tumours, pain that increases with physical activity and improves with re

params.question: In bone tumours, pain that increases with physical activity and improves with rest is the most important red flag for malignancy.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: That is not right. Pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest is characteristic of ordinary mechanical pain. The critical red flag for malignancy is pain that is constant, worsens at night, and persists despite rest — the opposite of the mechanical pattern.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Activity-related pain that eases with rest is typical of mechanical or sports injuries. The hallmark red flag for bone tumour pain is that it is constant, worsens at night, and does not improve with rest. This pattern of rest pain and night pain is what should prompt urgent investigation.

interactions.label: Why is a CT scan of the chest considered mandatory in the staging workup of a pr

params.question: Why is a CT scan of the chest considered mandatory in the staging workup of a primary malignant bone tumour?

answers.text: It best demonstrates the extent of the primary tumour's soft-tissue involvement

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Soft-tissue extension is best assessed by MRI with contrast, which shows intramedullary extent, soft-tissue margins, and skip lesions with superior resolution. CT chest serves a different purpose in the staging workup.

answers.text: The lungs are the most common site of haematogenous spread from primary bone malignancies

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Osteosarcoma and Ewing's sarcoma spread haematogenously, and the lungs are by far the most common site for distant metastases. Detecting pulmonary deposits at staging changes both prognosis and the treatment plan.

answers.text: It is needed to evaluate mediastinal lymph node involvement as a prognostic marker

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Primary bone tumours predominantly spread via the bloodstream to the lungs, not via lymphatic drainage to mediastinal nodes. Lymph node staging is not a typical indication for CT chest in bone tumour workup.

answers.text: It measures the tumour's metabolic activity through contrast enhancement

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Metabolic activity is assessed by PET-CT using a radiolabelled glucose tracer, not by standard CT chest. CT chest is specifically indicated to detect pulmonary metastases.

overallFeedback.feedback: The lungs are the most common destination for haematogenous metastases from primary bone tumours. That is why CT chest is a mandatory part of every staging workup, alongside MRI of the primary site and a bone scan.
Well done. Recognising that the lungs are the most common metastatic target is key to understanding why CT chest is mandatory, not optional, in every bone tumour staging workup.

interactions.label: A patient presents with inability to oppose the thumb following a deep laceratio

params.question: A patient presents with inability to oppose the thumb following a deep laceration at the wrist. Which nerve is most likely injured, and what is the resulting deformity called?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ulnar nerve injury produces claw hand — hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints of the ring and little fingers — not loss of thumb opposition. The ulnar nerve is vulnerable at the medial epicondyle or Guyon's canal.

Correct. The median nerve supplies the thenar muscles responsible for thumb opposition. Injury at the wrist, including carpal tunnel lacerations, produces ape hand deformity where the thumb lies flat and cannot oppose. An opponens splint maintains the thumb in a functional position during recovery.

Radial nerve injury causes wrist drop due to paralysis of the wrist and finger extensors. It does not affect thumb opposition, which is a function of the thenar muscles innervated by the median nerve.

The posterior interosseous nerve is a deep branch of the radial nerve affecting finger and thumb extension at the metacarpophalangeal joints. It does not supply the thenar muscles, so thumb opposition remains intact.

overallFeedback.feedback: Loss of thumb opposition is the hallmark of median nerve injury, producing ape hand deformity. Remember the triad: mechanism (wrist laceration), motor deficit (loss of opposition), and sensory loss (thumb, index, and middle fingers).
Excellent. Matching the clinical deficit to the injured nerve is the foundation of peripheral nerve injury diagnosis. Loss of thumb opposition always points to the median nerve.

interactions.label: When applying a cock-up splint for radial nerve palsy, what is the correct wrist

params.question: When applying a cock-up splint for radial nerve palsy, what is the correct wrist position?

answers.text: Full flexion to rest the paralysed extensor muscles

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Full flexion is the very position the splint must prevent. With the extensors paralysed, the unopposed flexors pull the wrist into flexion. Leaving it there causes a fixed flexion contracture that persists even after nerve recovery.

answers.text: Neutral position with all finger joints immobilised in extension

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neutral position provides inadequate extension to counteract the pull of the intact flexor muscles. Additionally, immobilising the fingers causes joint stiffness — the finger joints must remain completely free to move.

answers.text: 30 to 40 degrees of extension with the finger joints free to move

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The cock-up splint holds the wrist in 30 to 40 degrees of extension, counteracting the pull of the unopposed flexors, while keeping all finger joints completely free. This maintains a functional hand position and prevents fixed flexion contracture during nerve recovery.

answers.text: 90 degrees of extension with all joints immobilised

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: 90 degrees of hyperextension is excessive and risks soft-tissue injury. The correct angle is 30 to 40 degrees. Furthermore, immobilising all joints would cause widespread stiffness — only the wrist is held; the fingers must move freely.

overallFeedback.feedback: The cock-up splint must hold the wrist in 30 to 40 degrees of extension while keeping all finger joints free to move. Positional precision is what makes the splint therapeutic rather than harmful.

Well done. Precise positioning — 30 to 40 degrees of wrist extension with free finger movement — is what makes the cock-up splint effective. A splint in the wrong position causes the very contracture it was meant to prevent.

interactions.label: A 17-year-old presents with fever, raised ESR, and a warm tender swelling over t

params.question: A 17-year-old presents with fever, raised ESR, and a warm tender swelling over the mid-shaft of the femur. X-ray shows a permeative lytic lesion with onion-skin periosteal layering. Blood cultures are negative. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Start empirical intravenous antibiotics and observe the clinical response

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While osteomyelitis is in the differential, starting antibiotics without a tissue diagnosis could mask an underlying Ewing's sarcoma and delay definitive chemotherapy. When two diagnoses are equally plausible, histological confirmation must come first.

answers.text: Perform a bone biopsy at a specialist centre

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Ewing's sarcoma and osteomyelitis can present almost identically — fever, local warmth, raised inflammatory markers, and even similar radiological findings. With negative blood cultures, clinical features alone cannot distinguish them. A core needle biopsy provides the definitive histological diagnosis needed to guide treatment.

answers.text: Repeat the X-ray in two weeks to reassess the lesion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A two-week delay is inappropriate when a highly aggressive malignancy is in the differential. Ewing's sarcoma requires prompt diagnosis and neoadjuvant chemotherapy — waiting for radiological progression wastes critical time.

answers.text: Begin neoadjuvant chemotherapy based on the radiological appearance alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Starting chemotherapy without histological confirmation is inappropriate. Although the onion-skin periosteal reaction raises suspicion for Ewing's sarcoma, the same features can occur in osteomyelitis. A tissue diagnosis must be established before initiating any specific treatment.

overallFeedback.feedback: Ewing's sarcoma is called the 'great imitator' because it mimics osteomyelitis with fever, warmth, and raised inflammatory markers. When the two cannot be distinguished clinically, a bone biopsy at a specialist centre is the essential next step.

Excellent clinical reasoning. When Ewing's sarcoma and osteomyelitis are both plausible and blood cultures are negative, biopsy at a specialist centre is the only reliable way to distinguish them and guide definitive treatment.
